content: Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a virus belonging to the enterovirus genus within the Picornaviridae family. It is a non-enveloped virus with a positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome. EV-D68 is primarily transmitted through aerosolized respiratory droplets or direct contact with infected individuals. Historically considered a rare infection, its prevalence has been increasing in recent years. While it was initially thought to predominantly affect children, recent evidence suggests that adults are also significantly affected. Unlike most other enteroviruses, EV-D68 almost exclusively causes respiratory illnesses. Common symptoms include coughing, difficulty breathing (dyspnea), and wheezing. When evaluating patients with these symptoms, EV-D68 should be considered alongside other respiratory pathogens such as respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, parainfluenza virus, influenza B, coronavirus, and rhinovirus. Diagnosis is typically confirmed using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) testing of oral or nasopharyngeal swab specimens. Most cases are managed with supportive care on an outpatient basis, but severe cases, particularly in individuals at the extremes of age or those with pre-existing pulmonary or systemic conditions, may require hospitalization, oxygen therapy, or mechanical ventilation. EV-D68 was first identified in 1962 in California, where it was isolated from four hospitalized children with pneumonia and bronchiolitis. Although it remained a rare disease for decades, a significant outbreak occurred in the United States in September 2014, affecting 10 states, including Colorado, North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Kentucky. The virus exhibits a strong preference for infecting respiratory mucosal cells and leukocytes. Its ability to replicate within leukocytes facilitates its spread to other tissues, increases viral load, and activates endothelial cells, which attract additional leukocytes to the site of infection. EV-D68 is acid-labile and grows optimally at lower temperatures, which may explain its predilection for the respiratory tract. The virus recognizes specific cell surface receptors, including the Decay-Accelerating Factor (DAF) and sialic acid-containing receptors, to facilitate entry into host cells. The genome of EV-D68 consists of a single open reading frame (ORF) that encodes a polyprotein, which is subsequently cleaved into various structural and non-structural viral proteins. Viral serotyping is based on the VP1 gene, which encodes one of the four capsid proteins. Recent genetic studies have revealed rearrangements and deletions in the viral genome, particularly in untranslated regions (UTRs), leading to the classification of the virus into distinct clades. Differentiating EV-D68 from other respiratory infections is critical, as it shares symptoms such as fever, cough, malaise, and rhinorrhea with other pathogens, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, parainfluenza virus, influenza B, coronavirus, and rhinovirus. Although EV-D68 is considered rare, its true incidence and prevalence remain unclear. Recent data indicate an increase in reported cases. While earlier studies suggested that children aged 4 to 5 years were most commonly affected, newer evidence points to a higher prevalence among adults. Males appear to be more frequently affected, with no significant differences observed across racial or ethnic groups. Risk factors for EV-D68 infection include poor hygiene practices, such as failing to cover the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing and inadequate handwashing. Individuals at the extremes of age, as well as those with pulmonary conditions like asthma or cystic fibrosis or systemic comorbidities, are at higher risk for severe disease. The natural history of EV-D68 infection is not well understood due to limited data. The clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic cases to severe respiratory symptoms requiring hospitalization. While the prognosis is generally favorable, complications such as superimposed bacterial infections and severe pneumonia necessitating mechanical ventilation have been reported. These complications are more common in patients at the extremes of age or those with pre-existing pulmonary or systemic conditions. Patients with EV-D68 infection typically present with symptoms of acute upper or lower respiratory tract infection. Common symptoms include cough, difficulty breathing, and fever. On physical examination, findings may include fever, rapid breathing (tachypnea), skin rash, erythematous tonsils without exudates, and wheezing. Laboratory findings often reveal leukocytosis with a predominance of lymphocytes. RT-PCR testing of oral or nasopharyngeal swabs is the most reliable diagnostic method. Viral culture is less commonly performed but can confirm the presence of the virus. Serological tests have low sensitivity and are not routinely used for diagnosis. Chest X-rays may be ordered for patients with lower respiratory tract symptoms. Abnormal findings may include infiltrates, consolidation, atelectasis, and air trapping. There is no specific antiviral treatment for EV-D68. Most patients can be managed on an outpatient basis with supportive care. Severe cases may require hospitalization, intensive care, and mechanical ventilation. Although no specific therapies for EV-D68 exist, investigational treatments are being explored. Immune globulin therapy has shown some benefit in enterovirus infections, and antiviral agents like pleconaril are under investigation for severe cases caused by other enterovirus subtypes.
